name: Timsort (gfx::timsort, cpp-TimSort)
baseline: std::sort and std::stable_sort (also std::inplace_merge for gfx::timmerge)
workload: Sorting 100000-element int and std::string sequences that are randomized, reversed or already sorted; merging two sorted runs of 100000 elements for int and std::string.
claimed_speedup: README benchmark (timing scale: sec., size 100000): reversed int std::sort 0.045461 vs timsort 0.019139 (about 2.4x faster, derived from page data); sorted int 0.021876 vs 0.008042 (about 2.7x, derived); reversed std::string 0.586707 vs 0.345099 (about 1.7x, derived); sorted std::string 0.402458 vs 0.298639 (about 1.3x, derived); against std::stable_sort, reversed int 0.575431 vs 0.019139 (about 30x, derived). On randomized data timsort is SLOWER: int std::sort 0.695253 vs timsort 1.255825, std::string 3.438217 vs 5.791845. Merge benchmark (ms): sorted std::string std::inplace_merge 158.238114 vs timmerge 0.273858 (about 578x, derived), reversed int 11.441404 vs 4.017482, randomized int 33.404430 vs 37.047990 (timmerge slower).
compiler_and_flags: Sort run: Apple LLVM 7.0.0 (clang-700.0.72), c++ -Wall -Wextra -g -DNDEBUG -O2 -std=c++11 example/bench.cpp. Merge run: GCC 10.2.0 on Linux (Manjaro per the wiki page), c++ -Wall -Wextra -g -DNDEBUG -O2 -std=c++11 bench_merge.cpp. Standard libraries inferred from the toolchains (Apple clang on darwin uses libc++, GCC on Linux uses libstdc++), not stated.
hardware: CPU model not stated (target x86_64-apple-darwin14.5.0 for the sort run, x86_64-pc-linux-gnu for the merge run)
stars_or_usage: 319 stars; on Conan Center as timsort
tradeoffs: Stable O(n log n) sort that needs extra heap memory and cannot fall back to an O(n log^2 n) in-place algorithm when allocation is short. Slower than std::sort on random data. Version 3.x requires C++20 (ranges, projections); branches 2.x.y (C++11) and 1.x.y (C++03) are no longer actively maintained.
caveats: Tier C: the project's own benchmark code with no CPU model and no standard-library statement. The README sort output was produced with Apple LLVM 7.0.0 (2015 toolchain) at -O2 and the README states plainly that timsort is slower than std::ranges::sort on randomized sequences and faster only on partially-sorted ones, so the win is limited to presorted, reversed or nearly sorted inputs (the awesome-cpp listing says the same). The sort numbers come from the old C++11 example/bench.cpp, not necessarily the current benchmarks directory built with -DBUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON. Baseline is std::sort for the 'faster' rows, which is not stable; the fair stable baseline is std::stable_sort (also beaten on reversed and sorted input, and also slower on random input). The repo moved from gfx/cpp-TimSort to timsort/cpp-TimSort; the old URL redirects. The wiki page for the merge benchmark (https://github.com/timsort/cpp-TimSort/wiki/Benchmark-results) lists only the representative rows and GCC 10.2.0 / Manjaro / x86_64 with no CPU model.
found_via: seed-record pass: lead page https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Sorting (listing says 'outperforms quicksort-based algorithms including std::sort, for reversed or semi-sorted data'), then the repo README at https://github.com/timsort/cpp-TimSort and its wiki Benchmark-results page

name: TurboRLE (TRLE and SRLE)
baseline: rle8 (rainerzufalldererste/rle8, SSE/AVX2 8-bit run length encoder) and Mespotine RLE (MRLE); memcpy shown as a reference row
workload: Single-thread run length encode and decode throughput (MB/s) and compressed size on three large files: girl.bmp (RLE64Samples), a checkers end-game tablebase file (1034.db), and enwik9 after a Burrows-Wheeler transform (enwik9bwt), measured with TurboBench.
claimed_speedup: README claim: 'Compress better and up to 12 times faster and decompress up to 6 times faster than other fast RLEs'; 'Can be faster than memcpy!'. Skylake table (MB/s, C = compress, D = decompress): girl.bmp trle C 2089 / D 11385, srle 8 C 11307 / D 13205 (4744806 bytes) vs rle8 C 890 / D 11998 (5901235 bytes) and mrle C 378 / D 12302; enwik9bwt trle C 472 / D 1743, srle 8 C 568 / D 4310 vs rle8 C 260 / D 675 and mrle C 207 / D 553; 1034.db trle C 774 / D 3020 vs rle8 C 456 / D 2669 and mrle C 262 / D 1491. Derived from page data: srle 8 compresses girl.bmp about 12.7x faster than rle8 and decompresses enwik9bwt about 6.4x faster than rle8; trle compresses girl.bmp about 2.3x faster than rle8 while decompressing slightly slower (11385 vs 11998 MB/s). srle 64 compresses girl.bmp at 16269 MB/s vs memcpy 13978 MB/s (output is larger, 19839711 bytes).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 8.3 (tables dated 2019-08); flags not stated in the README. The current TurboBench makefile builds the TurboRLE objects with -O3 -march=haswell -w -fstrict-aliasing -falign-loops=32 -DNDEBUG on x86_64, but that is the HEAD makefile, not the 2019 revision, and the rle8 baseline object flags are not shown the same way.
hardware: Intel Skylake i7-6700 3.4GHz (x86 tables); ARM A73 ODROID-N2 1.8GHz (second set of tables, same ordering)
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0-or-later (copyleft; a commercial licence is not described in the README). Pure C with no inline assembly, SIMD paths for SSE/AVX2/NEON plus a RISC-V scalar fallback, and Java JNI bindings. Several variants (srle 8/16/32/64) trade compression ratio for speed, so the fastest rows compress much worse than rle8 or mrle: the 12x and 6x figures pair different output sizes.
caveats: Tier C because the benchmark tables are first-party, dated 2019-08, with the compiler version and CPU stated but no flags in the README (TurboBench is public, so a verifier may be able to raise this to A by reproducing from the makefile). The baselines are other RLE libraries, not a stdlib facility; 'up to' numbers cherry-pick the best variant per file (srle 8 vs rle8 on girl.bmp; srle 8 decompress vs rle8 on enwik9bwt). TurboRLE trle is slower than rle8 and mrle at decompression on girl.bmp (11385 vs 11998 and 12302 MB/s), so the 'decompress faster' claim does not hold on every file. The README table rows for rle8 and mrle show only one rle8 configuration (rle8 1). The memcpy row and the 'faster than memcpy' claim apply only to compression of highly compressible data.
found_via: seed-record pass: lead page https://github.com/oz123/awesome-c (listing 'Most efficient run-length encoding'), then repo README and TurboBench makefile on raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Vc (SIMD Vector Classes)
baseline: plain sequential scalar loop built by GCC 5.3.0 with -O3 -ftree-vectorize -ffast-math (compiler auto-vectorization; exp/log/sqrt go through libm)
workload: Euro-Par 2016 SIMD kernels run on one thread over 8192 doubles with AVX2 (SIMD width 4): simple (sqrt/log/exp wrapper), conditional math call, early return, nested branching, and while loop with varying trip count; the Vc 1.2.0 version (simd_class_vectorization) is compared with the sequential reference.
claimed_speedup: Third-party data (mean time per loop iteration, GCC 5.3.0, Haswell, 1 thread, SIMD width 4), Vc vs sequential reference, ratios derived from page data: simple EXP 7.8586e-09 s vs 2.477e-08 s (3.15x), simple LOG 8.14221e-09 vs 3.58324e-08 (4.40x), simple SQRT 6.41381e-09 vs 1.14677e-08 (1.79x); conditional_math_call EXP 2.27x, LOG 2.39x, SQRT 5.07x (3.3077e-09 vs 1.67538e-08); early_return EXP 2.87x, LOG 3.16x, SQRT 4.30x; nested_branching EXP 1.56x, LOG 1.64x, SQRT 2.19x; while_loop EXP 1.34x, LOG 1.62x, SQRT 0.78x (Vc slower: 5.97054e-08 vs 4.6563e-08). Hand-written AVX2 intrinsics and OpenMP 4.x 'omp simd' versions are often equal or faster than Vc in the same logs.
compiler_and_flags: GNU 5.3.0 (glibc 2.22 era), Vc 1.2.0; makefile.gnu in flwende/simd_benchmarks: g++ -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++11 -ftree-vectorize -ffast-math -mavx2 -mfma -D__AVX2__ -DSIMD_WIDTH_LOGICAL_REAL64=4 -DDEBUG, built with -DCONDITIONAL_CALL (notes.txt). The makefile is the master-branch copy and may differ slightly from the August 2016 build.
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2680v3 (Haswell) at 1.9 GHz, Cray aprun with --p-state=1900000
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars; packaged in Debian and Arch Linux and listed in CERN LCG
tradeoffs: Explicit SIMD value types (float_v, double_v) written into the code, so algorithms must be restructured for data parallelism; supports x86 SSE2 to AVX2 only (AVX-512, NEON and MIC support removed or never finished); the project is in maintenance mode and points users to std-simd (std::experimental::simd in GCC 11+ libstdc++).
caveats: Vc's own README and docs carry no benchmark numbers; the evidence is third-party data from the Euro-Par 2016 paper 'Portable SIMD Performance with OpenMP 4.x Compiler Directives' (Wende et al.), whose subject is OpenMP, not Vc. The baseline is compiler-generated scalar code with libm calls, not a library facility: the reference loop's exp/log calls may not auto-vectorize on GCC 5.3.0 unless glibc libmvec is used (GLIBC_ROOT is optional in the makefile and notes.txt does not say whether it was set for the hsw runs), so the larger gains may partly measure Vc's vector math against scalar libm. Vc is slower than the reference on while_loop SQRT (0.78x), and only single-thread width-4 AVX2 logs were read here (threads12 and SIMD width 8 logs, Intel and Clang runs not read). The Vc authors' own paper (Kretz and Lindenstruth, Software: Practice and Experience) and Kretz's dissertation were unreachable (host blocked), so no first-party numbers were checked. The data repo has only 9 commits and 6 stars.
found_via: seed-record pass: lead page https://github.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp#Math ('SIMD Vector Classes for C++'); the Vc repo README had no numbers; the benchmark data was found through a WebSearch hit for https://github.com/flwende/simd_benchmarks (OpenMP 4.x SIMD Benchmarks, which includes a Vc version)

name: Versor (geometric algebra library)
baseline: other C++ geometric algebra solutions: GluCat (framed and matrix), TbGAL, Garamon, Gaalet, Gaalop, GATL
workload: ga-benchmark: 10 unary and 12 binary geometric algebra operations (geometric product, outer product, inner products, dualization, inversion and others) on conformal, Euclidean (2-5 D) and Minkowski models plus a conformal inverse kinematics algorithm, ranked by mean CPU time with Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: ga-benchmark medal table (using mean time), 2020-02-05 run, gold/silver/bronze counts out of 323 comparisons per solution: GATL 247/75/1, Versor 246/76/1, Gaalop 246/18/0 (59 compilation errors), Gaalet 238/26/0 (59 compilation errors), TbGAL 34 gold / 56 silver / 97 bronze, Garamon 26/255/42, GluCat (framed) 6/60/151, GluCat (matrix) 0/3/45. Versor ties GATL for the lead and wins far more golds than Garamon, TbGAL and GluCat; the table gives no per-operation time ratios.
compiler_and_flags: GNU Compiler Collection 7.4.0 in 'release' mode (CMake Release; exact flags not stated in the result pages)
hardware: 8 x 1992 MHz CPUs, CPU model not stated, Linux 4.4.0-18362-Microsoft (Windows Subsystem for Linux), CPU scaling off, metric CPU time
stars_or_usage: 327 stars, 54 forks; one of seven solutions in ga-benchmark
tradeoffs: Template-metaprogramming library for Euclidean, Conformal, Projective and Minkowski geometric algebras with arbitrary metrics; needs C++11 (gcc 4.7+, clang 3.2+); heavy compile times were reported as improved in the README; includes OpenGL drawing helpers; the lead developer's PhD project.
caveats: Tier B: independent community suite (ga-developers/ga-benchmark, code public, run published in ga-benchmark-runs) but the page gives no CPU model and no compiler flags, and the run is from February 2020, so the Versor revision tested may differ from current devel. The result is a medal ranking against other geometric algebra libraries, not a speedup against a standard-library or BLAS incumbent; a tie with GATL (247 vs 246 gold) is not a win, and Gaalop and Gaalet counts are inflated by 59 compilation-error faults each. The suite lists Versor's homepage http://versor.mat.ucsb.edu as its source; that site was not opened (project sites are blocked per the harness notes) and the GitHub repo wolftype/Versor was used instead; its README makes only the claim '(fast)' with no numbers (the README 'SPEED' section is prose only). The suite's rendered results site (ga-developers.github.io) was not opened either; the table above was read from the ranking_1.html file checked into ga-benchmark-runs.
